Let $(S,\Sigma)$ and $(T_i,\Tau_i)$ for $i<n$ be measurable spaces, with
$n<\infty$, and let $K_i:S\to T_i$ be probability kernels with the same
source. There is a unique probability kernel
$$K:S\to\prod_{i<n}T_i$$
whose evaluation on every measurable rectangle is
$$K(s,\prod_{i<n}B_i)=\prod_{i<n}K_i(s,B_i).$$
For $n=0$, the target is the empty-product singleton and $K$ is its point
mass. For $n>0$, the product sigma-algebra is the recursive finite product
sigma-algebra.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]). Equip
$\overline{\mathbb R}$ ([[def-extended-reals]]) with its order topology and let
$\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ be the corresponding Borel sigma-algebra
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]).

A function $f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ is **measurable** when
$f^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

Equivalently, it is enough to require
$$\{x\in X:f(x)>a\}\in\mathcal A \qquad \text{for every } a\in\mathbb R,$$
because the rays $(a,+\infty]$ generate $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

Write $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the image of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$
under the canonical embedding $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), the
set usually written $\mathbb{Q}$ once the identification is made, and put
$X := \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the irrationals. Then:

1. $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, that is,
   $\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}} = \mathbb{R}$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]);
2. $X$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$;
3. every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
   ([[def-countable]]).

Claim 2 is not a symmetry of claim 1: the rationals are dense because they are
*constructed* to approximate, whereas the irrationals are dense because there are
too many points in any interval for a countable set to exhaust it, which is why
claim 3 is proved alongside and used for it.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

derivations.claim: The product kernel $K$ is a probability kernel by [F1]. Construct the finite product measure recursively: the one-factor case is $\nu_0$, and each next product is sigma-finite by [F2] applied to the preceding sigma-finite product and the next $\nu_j$. By [F7], each coordinate pullback $(s,t)\mapsto f_j(s,t_j)$ is measurable on $S\times\prod_{j<n}T_j$. For two nonnegative extended-measurable functions $u,v$ and $a\ge0$, $$\{uv>a\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q,\ q>0}\{u>q\}\cap\{v>a/q\};$$ when $uv>a$, one can choose a positive rational $q$ with $a/v<q<u$, with the evident choice of any $0<q<u$ when $a=0$; this also covers infinite factors and excludes a zero factor under the stated $0\cdot\infty=0$ convention. For $a<0$ the superlevel set is the whole domain. Thus finite multiplication preserves measurability by [F6], and $f$ is jointly measurable.

Fix $s$ and define $\lambda_s(A)=\int_A f(s,t)\,
u(dt)$. By [F4], $\lambda_s$ is a measure. Repeated Tonelli [F3] and the probability-kernel density identities give $$\lambda_s\!\left(\prod_{j<n}T_jight)=\int\prod_{j<n}f_j(s,t_j)\,d
u=\prod_{j<n}\int f_j(s,t_j)\,
u_j(dt_j)=\prod_{j<n}K_j(s,T_j)=1.$$ Hence $\lambda_s$ is a probability measure.

For a measurable rectangle $R=\prod_{j<n}B_j$, repeated Tonelli and the density identities yield $$\lambda_s(R)=\prod_{j<n}\int_{B_j}f_j(s,t_j)\,\nu_j(dt_j)=\prod_{j<n}K_j(s,B_j)=K(s,R),$$ where the last equality is [F1]. Rectangles form a generating pi-system containing the whole product. Both measures are probabilities by step 1.2 and [F1], so the constant exhaustion by the whole product has common finite mass one. [F5] therefore gives $\lambda_s=K(s,\cdot)$ on the full product sigma-algebra. This holds for every $s$, proving the density assertion.

Fix a finite group count $m\ge1$, a standard Borel hyperparameter space
$(H,\mathcal H)$, and a standard Borel parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$.
Let $\Pi$ be a probability measure on $(H,\mathcal H)$ and let
$$G:H\times\mathcal T\to[0,1]$$
be a probability kernel. For each $j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$, let
$(\mathcal Y_j,\mathcal A_j)$ be a measurable observation space, let $\nu_j$
be a sigma-finite measure on it, and let $K_j$ be a probability kernel from
$(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to $(\mathcal Y_j,\mathcal A_j)$ with a specified
jointly measurable density $f_j:\Theta\times\mathcal Y_j\to[0,\infty]$:
$$K_j(\theta,B)=\int_B f_j(\theta,y_j)\,\nu_j(dy_j)\qquad(B\in\mathcal A_j).$$

The **finite-group hierarchical model** is the following specified kernel
construction. First draw $\eta\sim\Pi$. Conditional on $\eta$, draw
$\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m$ from the finite product kernel
$$G_\eta^{\otimes m}(d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m)=\bigotimes_{j=1}^mG_\eta(d\theta_j).$$
Thus the group parameters are conditionally independent and have the same
conditional law $G_\eta$. Conditional on the parameter tuple, draw the group
observations from the product kernel $\bigotimes_{j=1}^mK_j(\theta_j,\cdot)$.
The product-kernel laws are probability kernels by
[[lem-finite-products-of-probability-kernels]]. For each fixed $\eta$, the
coordinate maps under $G_\eta^{\otimes m}$ are independent random elements,
so their joint law is the finite product law
([[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]).

Put $\Xi=H\times\Theta^m$ with its finite product sigma-algebra. The proper
latent prior $P_0$ on $\Xi$ is
$$P_0(d\eta,d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m)=\Pi(d\eta)\prod_{j=1}^mG_\eta(d\theta_j),$$
well-defined by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. For
$\xi=(\eta,\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m)\in\Xi$, lift each observation kernel
to the common source $\Xi$ by
$$M_j(\xi,B)=K_j(\theta_j,B)\qquad(B\in\mathcal A_j).$$
The coordinate projection $\xi\mapsto\theta_j$ is measurable, so the kernel
definition shows that each $M_j$ is a probability kernel. Its specified
jointly measurable density is $(\xi,y_j)\mapsto f_j(\theta_j,y_j)$, by
composition with the same measurable coordinate projection. Let
$\mathcal Y=\prod_{j=1}^m\mathcal Y_j$,
$\nu=\bigotimes_{j=1}^m\nu_j$, and $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_m)$. The observation
kernel from $\Xi$ has jointly measurable density
$$L_y(\eta,\theta_1\cdots\theta_m)=\prod_{j=1}^m f_j(\theta_j,y_j)$$
with respect to $\nu$, by [[lem-finite-products-of-dominated-kernels-have-product-density]].
Its **evidence** is the possibly extended nonnegative number
$$Z(y)=\int_\Xi L_y(\eta,\theta_1\cdots\theta_m)\,P_0(d\eta,d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m).$$
The normalized likelihood measure is called a pointwise joint posterior on a
fiber only when $0<Z(y)<\infty$; no quotient is formed at zero or infinite
evidence.

For each group, $\theta\mapsto K_j(\theta,\cdot)$ is a parametric statistical
model in the sense of [[def-parametric-statistical-model]], with its
parameter-measurable kernel representation as in
[[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]. Here
“conditionally independent given $\eta$” is shorthand for the explicit
finite product-kernel specification above. The library's random-element
conditional-independence terminology is defined in
[[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]; its
conditional-expectation-class convention assumes AC. The finite
product-kernel definition here does not use that class convention or any
choice axiom.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable spaces,
let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel. For
$C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A$, write
$C_\theta=\{x\in\mathcal X:(\theta,x)\in C\}$ and set
$$J(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\pi(d\theta).$$
Then $J$ is a probability measure on the product sigma-algebra, and for every
nonnegative product-measurable $h$,
$$\int_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}h(\theta,x)\,J(d\theta,dx)=\int_\Theta\left(\int_\mathcal Xh(\theta,x)\,K(\theta,dx)\right)\pi(d\theta).$$
In particular, $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\pi(d\theta)$ for
$A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal A$.
Every finite product of standard Borel spaces, with its finite product sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.

Assume AC. Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable random element with standard-Borel target, and let $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be any sub-sigma-algebra. There exists a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\mathcal G$. Every section is a probability measure, including at exceptional sample points, and no countable-generation or completeness assumption on $\mathcal G$ is required.

For this necessarily nonempty target, the construction also supplies a bimeasurable bijection $c:E\to B$ onto a Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$, and a countable algebra $\mathcal A$ which generates $\mathcal S$, separates points, and determines finite measures.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The model definition supplies the proper latent prior $P_0$ on $\Xi$ and the probability kernel from $\Xi$ to the product observation space $\mathcal Y$; apply [F2] to obtain the joint probability law $P_0(d\xi)K(\xi,dy)$ on $\Xi\times\mathcal Y$. The definition of a regular conditional distribution requires every section to be a probability measure, including at exceptional sample points. The theorem asserts no normalization formula on a fixed observation fiber.

Proof applies standard-Borel existence only in the forward direction; having some RCD is not asserted to imply a standard-Borel latent target.

Coordinate maps are measurable; the finite latent target H x Theta^m is standard Borel. The cited RCD theorem requires AC and a standard-Borel target, but allows an arbitrary conditioning sub-sigma-algebra, so arbitrary observation spaces cause no gap. derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F3], the latent prior $P_0$ is a probability measure and the model kernel gives a joint probability law for the latent tuple and the observations. By [F2], that observation kernel is dominated by the sigma-finite product measure $\nu$ with the specified jointly measurable density $L(\xi,y)=\prod_j f_j(\theta_j,y_j)$. be a sigma-finite measure on it, and let $K_j$ be a probability kernel from

jointly measurable density $f_j:\Theta\times\mathcal Y_j\to[0,\infty]$:
$$K_j(\theta,B)=\int_B f_j(\theta,y_j)\,\nu_j(dy_j)\qquad(B\in\mathcal A_j).$$

$$f : X \times Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$$
be $(\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B,\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R}))$-measurable.
Then $f_x : Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal B$-measurable for every
$x \in X$, and $f^y : X \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable
for every $y \in Y$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(S,\Sigma)$ and $(T_i,\Tau_i)$ for $i<n$ be measurable spaces, with
$n<\infty$, and let $K_i:S\to T_i$ be probability kernels with the same
source. There is a unique probability kernel
$$K:S\to\prod_{i<n}T_i$$
whose evaluation on every measurable rectangle is
$$K(s,\prod_{i<n}B_i)=\prod_{i<n}K_i(s,B_i).$$
For $n=0$, the target is the empty-product singleton and $K$ is its point
mass. For $n>0$, the product sigma-algebra is the recursive finite product
sigma-algebra.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Fix a group $j$ and specialize [F5] to one observation: identify its parameter with $\theta_j$, set $\mu_0=\mu$, $\tau_0^2=\tau^2$, $n=1$, $y_1=\bar y_j$, and $\sigma^2=s_j^2$. The model and pointwise density specification in [F1] supply this normal prior and the canonical normal likelihood density used by [F5], while [A1] and [A2] verify the choice and positive-variance hypotheses of [F5]. The theorem gives a finite positive group evidence and posterior variance $V_j=(1/\tau^2+1/s_j^2)^{-1}$ and mean $\hat\theta_j=V_j(\mu/\tau^2+\bar y_j/s_j^2)$, as stated.

For each group put $\mu_j(A)=\int_A f_j(\theta,\bar y_j)N(\mu,\tau^2)(d\theta)$ and let $m_j=\mu_j(\mathbb R)>0$. By [F5] and step 1.1, $\mu_j/m_j=Q_j=N(\hat\theta_j,V_j)$. Apply [F3] to the hierarchy with the proper point-mass hyperprior at the fixed $(\mu,\tau^2)$. Its latent prior on $\mathbb R^m$ is the product of the group priors by [F1], and its likelihood density is $\prod_j f_j(\theta_j,\bar y_j)$ by [F2]. Repeated Tonelli [F4] shows that the normalized posterior assigns each measurable rectangle $\prod_j A_j$ mass $\prod_j\mu_j(A_j)/\prod_jm_j=\prod_jQ_j(A_j)$, the rectangle mass of $\bigotimes_jQ_j$ by [F9]. By [F8], rectangles form a generating pi-system. Both are probability measures agreeing on it; the constant exhaustion by the full space has common finite mass one, so [F6] makes them equal. This proves conditional independence and the displayed formula for every group.

Now suppose $(\mu,\tau^2)$ is random with a proper hyperprior supported on $H$. For fixed observed summaries, put $M_j((\mu,\tau^2),A)=\int_A f_j(\theta,\bar y_j)N(\mu,\tau^2)(d\theta)$. The factor $f_j(\cdot,\bar y_j)$ is measurable by the section fact [F8]; composing it with the parameter-coordinate projection shows that $(\eta,\theta)\mapsto1_A(\theta)f_j(\theta,\bar y_j)$ is product-measurable. Since $G_\eta=N(\mu,\tau^2)$ is a probability kernel, [F7] makes $M_j(\cdot,A)$ measurable. Hence $m_j=M_j(\cdot,\mathbb R)$ and $Q_j(A)=M_j(\cdot,A)/m_j$ are measurable, with $m_j>0$ by step 1.1. Repeated Tonelli [F4] and the full-posterior formula [F3] give, for measurable $C\subseteq H$ and $A_1,\ldots,A_m\subseteq\mathbb R$, $P_y(C\times\prod_jA_j)=Z(y)^{-1}\int_C\prod_jM_j((\mu,\tau^2),A_j)\,\Pi(d\mu,d\tau^2)$. Taking every $A_j=\mathbb R$ shows $\Pi_y(C)=Z(y)^{-1}\int_C\prod_jm_j\,d\Pi$. Taking only $A_j=A$ and all other sets equal to $\mathbb R$ therefore gives $P_y(\theta_j\in A)=\int_HQ_j(A)\,\Pi_y(d\mu,d\tau^2)$. By [F5] and step 1.1, $Q_j=N(\hat\theta_j,V_j)$, so the group posterior is its conditional normal law averaged over the full hyperparameter posterior. $$G_\eta^{\otimes m}(d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m)=\bigotimes_{j=1}^mG_\eta(d\theta_j).$$
Thus the group parameters are conditionally independent and have the same
conditional law $G_\eta$. Conditional on the parameter tuple, draw the group
observations from the product kernel $\bigotimes_{j=1}^mK_j(\theta_j,\cdot)$.

[[lem-finite-products-of-probability-kernels]]. For each fixed $\eta$, the
coordinate maps under $G_\eta^{\otimes m}$ are independent random elements,
so their joint law is the finite product law
([[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]).

latent prior $P_0$ on $\Xi$ is
$$P_0(d\eta,d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m)=\Pi(d\eta)\prod_{j=1}^mG_\eta(d\theta_j),$$

$\xi=(\eta,\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m)\in\Xi$, lift each observation kernel

$$M_j(\xi,B)=K_j(\theta_j,B)\qquad(B\in\mathcal A_j).$$

composition with the same measurable coordinate projection. Let
$\mathcal Y=\prod_{j=1}^m\mathcal Y_j$,

kernel from $\Xi$ has jointly measurable density
$$L_y(\eta,\theta_1\cdots\theta_m)=\prod_{j=1}^m f_j(\theta_j,y_j)$$
with respect to $\nu$, by [[lem-finite-products-of-dominated-kernels-have-product-density]].

$$Z(y)=\int_\Xi L_y(\eta,\theta_1\cdots\theta_m)\,P_0(d\eta,d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m).$$
The normalized likelihood measure is called a pointwise joint posterior on a
fiber only when $0<Z(y)<\infty$; no quotient is formed at zero or infinite
evidence.

model in the sense of [[def-parametric-statistical-model]], with its
parameter-measurable kernel representation as in
[[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]. Here

finite product-kernel specification above. The library's random-element
conditional-independence terminology is defined in
[[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]; its

product-kernel definition here does not use that class convention or any
choice axiom.

$$Z(y)=\int_\Xi L_y(\xi)\,P_0(d\xi).$$
